meta.subtitle: 750 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Dutch → English (see the Dutch, recall the meaning) and English → Dutch (see an English meaning, recall the Dutch). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words of Dutch for an elementary learner, aligned to A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to manage simple, routine exchanges of information on familiar matters — personal and family information, shopping, the local area, work — and to describe in simple terms their background, their surroundings and what they immediately need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Dutch has examinations at these levels — the inburgeringsexamen, the Staatsexamen NT2 and the CNaVT — but no graded word list for them was found published, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 424 of the 750 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — relatives and the people around you, jobs and study, clothes, more food and cooking, the rooms and furniture of a home, the town and its services, travel and holidays, nature, the seasons and the compass, animals, health and the body, feelings and character, free time and sport, telling what happened when, the higher numbers and quantities, and the everyday verbs of moving, dressing, cooking and doing — and the other 326 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Dutch, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a verb or an adjective added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword has its pronunciation beneath it in the International Phonetic Alphabet, Wiktionary's own. The 403 nouns are printed with their article — de or het — because nothing in a Dutch noun says which it takes, and they show their plural and diminutive; the 157 verbs show their past and past participle (eten, at, gegeten), and behind the All forms fold their present and past by person, imperative and participles. Real example sentences come with 748 of the 750 words, three apiece for 746 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, forms and pronunciation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
